title: George Floyd
intro: What the "homicide" ruling means, the evidence behind the doubt and how the courts handled it, the body-camera timeline, every step of the court file, the people involved and their documented ties, and comparable restraint deaths. Primary records only; nothing here states or suggests anyone's motive.

sections.title: What "manner of death: homicide" means
notes: "Homicide" on the death certificate is a medical classification, not a finding of guilt.

The Hennepin County Medical Examiner (Dr. Andrew Baker) ruled the manner of death Homicide. He gave the cause as "cardiopulmonary arrest complicating law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression."
He also listed as "other significant conditions": "arteriosclerotic and hypertensive heart disease; fentanyl intoxication; recent methamphetamine use."

The National Association of Medical Examiners (NAME) manner-of-death guide says homicide means a death that results from another person's volitional act. It says the term "neither indicates nor implies criminal intent." It also says deaths from law-enforcement restraint "may be classified as Homicide," even when the person was already vulnerable because of disease.
So the ME's "homicide" ruling did not decide whether Chauvin committed a crime. The jury and the courts decided that.
Under Minnesota law, Floyd's heart disease and drug use did not legally excuse the death.

Minnesota has long required only that the defendant's conduct be a "substantial causal factor." It does not have to be the sole cause. A victim's pre-existing condition does not break the chain (State v. Smith, 1962; State v. King, 1985; State v. Gatson, 2011).
The jury was instructed in exactly those terms. Judge Cahill had already written in October 2020 that "Floyd's pre-existing medical conditions cannot defeat causation."

sections.title: The case for doubt, and how the courts handled it
notes: The record contains real evidence behind the doubt, and the courts dealt with it on the record. The main points on the doubting side:
Dr. Baker's autopsy found no physical signs of asphyxia or strangulation: no petechiae and no neck-structure injury. This is in the charging complaint and in a May 26, 2020 prosecutor memo.
A June 1, 2020 prosecutor memo summarizes Baker as calling the fentanyl level (11 ng/mL) "pretty high" and a "fatal level … under normal circumstances."
At trial, Baker admitted that if Floyd had been found dead at home alone with that fentanyl level and no trauma, he would have certified a fentanyl death.
On the other side:

Three prosecution experts testified that the mechanism was low oxygen from prone restraint: pulmonologist Dr. Martin Tobin, forensic pathologist Dr. Lindsey Thomas, and cardiologist Dr. Jonathan Rich. The toxicologist testified that the methamphetamine level was in the bottom 5.9% of 3,271 DUI cases.
The Armed Forces Medical Examiner's office reviewed the case for the U.S. Department of Justice and concurred on cause and manner (homicide).

The jury convicted. Judge Cahill later heard the same experts himself in the Thao bench trial and wrote that Fowler's opinion was "unpersuasive." The Court of Appeals affirmed, and the Minnesota Supreme Court and U.S. Supreme Court declined review.

Most significant: in his federal plea agreement, Chauvin himself admitted "that his willful use of unreasonable force resulted in Mr. Floyd's bodily injury and death because his actions impaired Mr. Floyd's ability to obtain and maintain sufficient oxygen."

One nuance the record shows plainly: the prosecution's own experts did not describe the mechanism the same way. Baker described heart disease plus the stress of subdual, restraint and neck compression. Tobin, Thomas and Rich described asphyxia (low oxygen). All of them attributed the death to the restraint.

sections.title: The court file
notes: Charges, rulings, instructions, verdict, appeals and the federal case in detail
1.1 Charges
Original complaint, May 29, 2020 (State v. Chauvin, 27-CR-20-12646).
Count I: third-degree murder, Minn. Stat. § 609.195(a). Count II: second-degree manslaughter, § 609.205(1).
Approved by prosecutor Amy Sweasy (HCAO). Complainant: BCA SA Michelle Frascone. Signed by Judge Luis Bartolomei. Bail $500,000.

It quoted the ME's preliminary findings: "The autopsy revealed no physical findings that support a diagnosis of traumatic asphyxia or strangulation. Mr. Floyd had underlying health conditions including coronary artery disease and hypertensive heart disease. The combined effects of Mr. Floyd being restrained by the police, his underlying health conditions and any potential intoxicants in his system likely contributed to his death."

It said the knee was on Floyd's neck "for 8 minutes and 46 seconds." Later court findings put the full restraint at about 9 minutes 29 seconds (COA) and "more than nine minutes and twenty seconds" (Thao verdict).
Source: Court file.
Amended complaint, June 3, 2020.
Added Count I: second-degree unintentional murder while committing a felony (§ 609.19 subd. 2(1)), with third-degree assault as the predicate felony. Kept third-degree murder and manslaughter.
Approved by AAG Matthew Frank. Bail $1,000,000.
Third-degree murder reinstated.
After the Court of Appeals' March 5, 2021 order in A21-0354, applying State v. Noor, and the Supreme Court's denial of review, the count was reinstated on March 11, 2021.
The reinstatement order itself was not retrieved; see Open items.

The jury convicted on that count, but it was never adjudicated (sentencing order). The COA therefore did not reach Chauvin's challenge to it. The Minnesota Supreme Court later narrowed third-degree murder in State v. Noor, 964 N.W.2d 424 (Minn. 2021).
Statutes as in force in 2020 (revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2020/cite/…):

§ 609.19 subd. 2(1): "causes the death of a human being, without intent to effect the death of any person, while committing or attempting to commit a felony offense other than criminal sexual conduct in the first or second degree with force or violence or a drive-by shooting." Maximum 40 years.

§ 609.195(a): "Whoever, without intent to effect the death of any person, causes the death of another by perpetrating an act eminently dangerous to others and evincing a depraved mind, without regard for human life." Maximum 25 years.

§ 609.205(1): death caused "by the person's culpable negligence whereby the person creates an unreasonable risk, and consciously takes chances of causing death or great bodily harm to another." Maximum 10 years.
§ 609.223 subd. 1 (the predicate): "Whoever assaults another and inflicts substantial bodily harm." Maximum 5 years, so it is a felony.
§ 609.02 subd. 7a defines "substantial bodily harm" as including "a temporary but substantial loss or impairment of the function of any bodily member or organ."
For comparison: § 609.221 (first degree, great bodily harm) and § 609.222 (second degree, dangerous weapon).
1.2 Pretrial rulings on fairness

Venue. Preliminary order Nov. 4, 2020: "preliminarily DENIED"; "a change of venue is unlikely to cure the taint." The court said it would reconsider. It denied venue and continuance again in March 2021 after the settlement, stating "no county in the state can do more to ensure a fair trial than Hennepin" (quoted in the COA).
HCAO disqualification.

Defense motion Aug. 28, 2020 (Nelson). The court's Nov. 4, 2020 order vacated its Sept. 11, 2020 oral removal order. Freeman, LeFevour, Sweasy and Lofton "may not appear as advocates in the trials … and may not sign any motions or pleadings … but may otherwise participate."

"The sole reason for the removal Order was that the four attorneys discussed the case with … Dr. Andrew Baker, on May 27, 2020, without the presence of a non-attorney witness." The court clarified it meant "careless" rather than "sloppy."
Footnote 3 discloses the judge's own background: "As a former prosecutor in the Hennepin County Attorney's office … I have always found the attorneys … to be ethical."
Source: Court file.
1.3 Jury instructions (filed April 19, 2021): causation

"'To cause death' … means that the Defendant's act or acts were a substantial causal factor in causing the death of George Floyd. The Defendant is criminally liable for all the consequences of his actions that occur in the ordinary and natural course of events, including those consequences brought about by one or more intervening causes, if such intervening causes were the natural result of the Defendant's acts. The fact that other causes contribute to the death does not relieve the Defendant of criminal liability. However, the Defendant is not criminally liable if a 'superseding cause' caused the death. A 'superseding cause' is a cause that comes after the Defendant's acts, alters the natural sequence of events, and is the sole cause of a result that would not otherwise have occurred."
1.4 Verdict, aggravating factors and sentence
Verdicts, April 20, 2021 (forms filed April 21): guilty on all three counts (verdict1/2/3).

Proven beyond a reasonable doubt: abuse of a position of trust and authority; particular cruelty ("The slow death of George Floyd occurring over approximately six minutes of his positional asphyxia was particularly cruel"); children present; committed as a group with three others.
Not proven: particular vulnerability. The court wrote: "Mr. Floyd's drug intoxication did not render him particularly vulnerable compared to other victims of murder."

Sentencing order, June 25, 2021. Convicted on Count I only; Counts II and III unadjudicated (§ 609.04). Sentence 270 months against a presumptive 150 months (range 128–180). Appearing for the State: Ellison, Frank, Schleicher, Blackwell. For the defense: Eric Nelson and Amy Voss.
New-trial / Schwartz order, June 23–24, 2021. No abuse of discretion; no prosecutorial misconduct; no prima facie juror misconduct.
1.5 Appeals

Venue, continuance, sequestration (syllabus I): affirmed. Mitigating steps included 18 defense peremptory strikes versus 10 for the State (Chauvin left 3 unused), individual voir dire, and jurors' confirmations that they could decide on the evidence.
Settlement (March 12, 2021, during voir dire): the court "recalled the seven seated jurors and excused two jurors for cause."

April 12, 2021 sequestration motion after the Brooklyn Center shooting: denied. April 19, 2021 mistrial motion over pretrial publicity and Rep. Waters' remarks: denied. The COA records both, affirms the fairness rulings, and does not analyze the Waters remarks separately.

Officials' statements, footnote 4: Chauvin cited the MPD chief and public-safety commissioner calling it "murder." The COA said: "We acknowledge that these were not pure statements of fact but presupposed guilt. However, because the district court took numerous mitigating steps … we conclude that this properly eliminated any potential prejudice."
Juror 52:

The claim that he concealed attending the August 2020 Washington march was "contradicted by the record." The questionnaire asked about demonstrations "in Minneapolis after [] Floyd's death," and he answered "no" truthfully.
His negative views of MPD were disclosed in voir dire.
Post-verdict media statements "must be viewed skeptically."
Chauvin could have used his unused strikes on him. Denying a Schwartz hearing was not an abuse of discretion.
Juror 96 was an alternate who did not deliberate.
Felony murder with an assault predicate for police (syllabus II): affirmed.
Instructions, evidentiary rulings and sentencing departure: affirmed.
Counsel on appeal: State, Ellison and Katyal. Chauvin, William Mohrman.
Minnesota Supreme Court denied review on July 18, 2023 (cert. appendix). U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari on Nov. 20, 2023 (No. 23-416).
1.6 Federal case (U.S. v. Chauvin, D. Minn., 0:21-cr-108 PAM/TNL; Judge Paul Magnuson)
Plea agreement (Doc. 142, Dec. 15, 2021):
Chauvin "willfully deprived George Perry Floyd, Jr., of his constitutional rights."

"As Mr. Floyd lay on the ground, handcuffed and unresisting, the defendant kept his knees on Floyd's neck and body, even after Mr. Floyd became unresponsive. This offense resulted in bodily injury to, and the death of George Floyd."

"The defendant admits that his willful use of unreasonable force resulted in Mr. Floyd's bodily injury and death because his actions impaired Mr. Floyd's ability to obtain and maintain sufficient oxygen to sustain Mr. Floyd's life."
Base offense level: second-degree murder. The plea also covered a Sept. 4, 2017 juvenile count.
Judgment (Doc. 529): imposed July 7, 2022. 252 months, adjusted to 245 for time served, concurrent with the state sentence.
Co-defendants:
Federal: Thao, Kueng and Lane were convicted by a federal jury (trial Jan. 24–Feb. 2022). Magnuson sentenced them to 42, 36 and 30 months (recited in the Thao verdict).

sections.title: People and their documented ties
notes: The people behind the case have ordinary political and professional ties. None rises to a documented conflict.
Judge Peter Cahill was appointed in 2007 by Republican Governor Tim Pawlenty. He was a long-time Hennepin County prosecutor, including chief deputy from 2000 to 2006.

Prosecutors Jerry Blackwell, Steven Schleicher and Lola Velázquez-Aguilu, and AG Keith Ellison (DFL), gave money to DFL/Democratic candidates. That includes Blackwell's contributions to Ellison's own AG campaign in 2018–2019 and to Gov. Walz. Blackwell was later appointed a federal judge by President Biden (confirmed 51–43, December 2022).
Neal Katyal gave to Democrats, including Biden 2020.
Federal Judge Paul Magnuson was appointed by Republican President Reagan (1981). No FEC or Minnesota contributions were found for him, for defense lawyer Eric Nelson, or for AAG Matthew Frank.
None of these ties was the subject of a recusal motion or a court finding in the record reviewed.
Ties are listed as facts. None was the subject of a recusal motion or court finding in the records reviewed. Unconfirmed contributor identities are not listed.
sections.label: Verified by SwampForce

sections.title: Documented conflicts or improprieties: the complete list
notes: One documented ruling. Judge Cahill's Nov. 4, 2020 order limited Hennepin County Attorney Freeman and assistants LeFevour, Sweasy and Lofton. They could not act as trial advocates or sign pleadings, because of an advocate-witness problem created by their May 27, 2020 meeting with Dr. Baker without a non-attorney witness. The court called this "careless." It is not a finding of bias, dishonesty or evidence tampering.
One judicial rebuke on the record (not a ruling against a party). Judge Cahill called officials' public comments on the case during trial "abhorrent," referring to Rep. Waters, and denied a mistrial.
One appellate acknowledgment. The Court of Appeals said the police chief's and public-safety commissioner's pre-trial "murder" statements "presupposed guilt," but held that any prejudice was cured.

No other conflicts or improprieties were found in the primary records reviewed. There was no recusal motion against either judge, no finding of bias by any court, no finding of juror misconduct (juror 52's claim was rejected on the record), and no finding of prosecutorial misconduct (the June 2021 new-trial order found none). Campaign contributions, prior employment and appointments listed in the ties table above are ordinary ties with no court finding attached.

sections.title: Outside pressure and how the courts responded
notes: Outside pressure was documented, and the courts ruled on each instance.

Rep. Maxine Waters (April 17, 2021) said "we're looking for a guilty verdict" and that protesters should "get more confrontational." Judge Cahill denied a mistrial, called officials' comments "abhorrent," and said Waters "may have given you something on appeal." On appeal, the conviction was affirmed.
President Biden (April 20, 2021), during deliberations, said the evidence was "overwhelming, in my view," noting that he said so only because the jury was sequestered.
The $27 million Minneapolis settlement (announced March 12, 2021, during jury selection): the court recalled the seven jurors already seated and excused two of them.

Juror 52: the Court of Appeals found the claim that he hid his attendance at the August 2020 Washington march "contradicted by the record." The questionnaire asked only about demonstrations in Minneapolis.

The Court of Appeals acknowledged that pre-trial statements by the Minneapolis police chief and public-safety commissioner calling it "murder" "presupposed guilt." It held that jury screening removed any prejudice.
Every venue, continuance, sequestration and new-trial request was denied, and those denials were affirmed.

sections.title: Comparable restraint deaths
notes: Pattern, stated honestly:
Medical examiners commonly classify restraint deaths as homicide even when drugs or heart disease are present (Floyd, Garner, Timpa, Prude, Ellis). This is consistent with the NAME guidance.
A homicide classification did not predict criminal conviction. Four of those five produced no criminal conviction.
A non-homicide classification did not prevent conviction (McClain).
"Accident" rulings exist (Quinto) and came from a coroner's inquest jury, not a board-certified ME's certificate.
The Floyd case stands out for the length of the video-recorded restraint, the clinical testimony on low oxygen, and the defendant's own federal admission of causation.
This is a small, non-random set of well-known cases, not a statistical sample.

sections.title: Officials' documented 2020 actions
notes: Minneapolis City Council, June 12, 2020. Resolution 2020R-152 (proceedings pp. 472–474) was adopted 12–0.
It declared the intent "to create a transformative new model for cultivating safety" and created a Future of Community Safety Work Group.
Its preamble reads: "the murder of George Floyd on May 25, 2020, by Minneapolis police officers."

That is an official act characterizing the death as murder about ten months before trial. The COA's footnote 4 addressed similar statements by the police chief and public-safety commissioner, not this resolution.
Charter amendment (LIMS 2020-00668; primary author Jeremiah Ellison). Notice given June 12, 2020 (12–0). Introduced and referred June 26, 2020 (12–0).
Charter Commission (CH2020-00014). Voted to take 90 more days on Aug. 5, 2020 (10–5), which kept the amendment off the Nov. 2020 ballot. Recommended rejection on Nov. 4, 2020 (14–0).
Nov. 2, 2021, City Question 2 (Department of Public Safety to replace the charter Police Department): Failed. Yes 62,813 (43.83%), No 80,506 (56.17%) (City of Minneapolis official results).

Bail funds: Sen. Kamala Harris, June 1, 2020 (2:34 p.m. MDT): "If you're able to, chip in now to the @MNFreedomFund to help post bail for those protesting on the ground in Minnesota." The Minnesota Freedom Fund's 2020 Form 990 reports about $10M in criminal bail for about 610 people, with no breakdown for protest arrests.
Officials' statements on guilt before trial (primary records found):
AG Ellison (June 3, 2020 release): "the murder of Mr. Floyd."
Minneapolis City Council (2020R-152): "the murder of George Floyd."
The police chief, public-safety commissioner and mayor (identified in the defense's venue memo and the COA; the COA says they "presupposed guilt").
President Biden (April 20, 2021, during deliberations).
The courts held that jury selection and instructions cured any prejudice.

floyd-1.title: The sources
lines: NAME, A Guide for Manner of Death Classification (1st ed., Feb. 2002; Hanzlick, Hunsaker, Davis):

"Homicide occurs when death results from a volitional act committed by another person to cause fear, harm, or death. Intent to cause death is a common element but is not required … the classification of Homicide for the purposes of death certification is a 'neutral' term and neither indicates nor implies criminal intent, which remains a determination within the province of legal processes."
"the manner of death is unnatural when injury hastened the death of one already vulnerable to significant or even life-threatening disease."

"Deaths due to positional restraint induced by law enforcement personnel or to choke holds or other measures to subdue may be classified as Homicide. In such cases, there may not be intent to kill, but the death results from one or more intentional, volitional, potentially harmful acts directed at the decedent."
more: The same passage adds that the classification has "some value … toward reducing the public perception that a 'cover up' is being perpetrated."

"Seldom, for the purpose of manner-of-death classification, is 'beyond a reasonable doubt' required." Death-certificate findings "only represent the certifier's opinion and are not written in stone or legally binding."
Hennepin County ME press release (June 1, 2020): "Manner of death is not a legal determination of culpability or intent."
New York AG Prude report (2021), same principle: the ME's homicide designation "is not a legal culpability determination"; it means the death occurred "at the hands of another."
CDC/NCHS Medical Examiners' and Coroners' Handbook on Death Registration (2003): the file could not be retrieved. It is not quoted here.
Minnesota causation law (quoted in the Oct. 21, 2020 probable-cause order):
A defendant's act is a substantial causal factor if it "contributed to the death" (State v. Torkelson, 404 N.W.2d 352, 357 (Minn. App. 1987)).
The State need not prove "the specific mechanism of death," and the act need not be "the sole cause of death" (State v. Gatson, 801 N.W.2d 134, 148 (Minn. 2011)).

State v. Smith, 119 N.W.2d 838, 848 (Minn. 1962): "It is immaterial that defendant did not know that the deceased was suffering from a condition which facilitated the killing … Responsibility attaches for an injury which causes or contributes to death although the condition from which the victim was suffering might itself have caused death in time."
State v. King, 367 N.W.2d 599, 602 (Minn. App. 1985): the victim's physical condition "will not excuse or minimize its consequences."
State v. James, 144 N.W. 216 (Minn. 1913): pneumonia after a stabbing.
A superseding cause must be "the sole cause" (Gatson; State v. Jaworsky, 505 N.W.2d 638).
The court concluded: "In short, Floyd's pre-existing medical conditions cannot defeat causation."
floyd-1.label: Verified by SwampForce

floyd-2.title: Dr. Andrew Baker
lines: Opinion / key testimony: Subdual, restraint and neck compression were "just more than Mr. Floyd could take by virtue of those heart conditions." Drugs were not "the direct cause." Paraganglioma did not have "anything to do with his death." Carbon monoxide "played no role." Conceded: at home alone with no trauma and that fentanyl level, he "would certify his death as due to fentanyl toxicity," but video and investigation matter "because the answers are not always obvious at the autopsy table alone."
floyd-2.label: Verified by SwampForce

floyd-3.title: Dr. Lindsey Thomas
lines: Opinion / key testimony: Asphyxia was the primary mechanism. Agreed with homicide. Floyd would not have died "except for the interactions with law enforcement."
floyd-3.label: Verified by SwampForce

floyd-4.title: Dr. Martin Tobin
lines: Opinion / key testimony: Lost consciousness by 8:24:53; last breath 8:25:16; oxygen at zero by 8:25:41. Respiratory rate about 22 before losing consciousness, inconsistent with fentanyl depression. Not a paraganglioma death.
floyd-4.label: Verified by SwampForce

floyd-5.title: Daniel Isenschmid
lines: Opinion / key testimony: Methamphetamine 19 ng/mL was "very low," in the bottom 5.9% of 3,271 DUI cases (mean 378, median 240). Fentanyl 11, norfentanyl 5.6.
floyd-5.label: Verified by SwampForce

floyd-6.title: Dr. Jonathan Rich
lines: Opinion / key testimony: "died from a cardiopulmonary arrest... caused by low oxygen levels" "induced by the prone restraint and positional asphyxiation." Ruled out a primary heart event "with a high degree of medical certainty." "every indicator is that Floyd had an exceptionally strong heart."
floyd-6.label: Verified by SwampForce

floyd-7.title: Dr. Vincent Bebarta
lines: Opinion / key testimony: Fentanyl 11 was "low." Overdose deaths "typically have levels of 40 ng/mL or higher." Asphyxia.
floyd-7.label: Verified by SwampForce

floyd-8.title: Dr. David Fowler
lines: Opinion / key testimony: "[c]ardiac arrhythmia due to hypertensive atherosclerotic disease during restraint." Contributors: carbon monoxide, methamphetamine, fentanyl, paraganglioma (Chauvin Tr. 5475). He acknowledged he "is not a toxicologist, pulmonologist, or cardiologist" (5579). Conceded he had no carbon monoxide lab result, that the methamphetamine level was "very low," that there were no overdose signs, and that Floyd needed "immediate emergency attention."
floyd-8.label: Verified by SwampForce

floyd-9.title: Cause-of-death testimony
lines: Judge Cahill's own assessment in the Thao bench trial found Baker, Tobin and Isenschmid credible. He found Fowler "unpersuasive" because he "lacks expertise and clinical experience in pulmonology, cardiology, and toxicology."
Early prosecutor memos, filed as exhibits in State v. Thao on Aug. 25, 2020:
May 26, 2020 (Lofton): "The autopsy revealed no physical evidence suggesting that Mr. Floyd died of asphyxiation." Baker "specifically avoided watching any videos … to avoid a bias."

June 1, 2020 (Sweasy): Baker described fentanyl 11 as "pretty high." The memo, in the author's words, says "That is a fatal level of fentanyl under normal circumstances." Baker said that "if Mr. Floyd had been found dead in his home … and there were no other contributing factors he would conclude that it was an overdose death."
more: These are memo authors' summaries written before Baker completed his investigation, not Baker's sworn testimony.

Armed Forces Medical Examiner (DoD Case Consult C0022-20, June 10, 2020, requested by DOJ; filed as a court exhibit): cause as Hennepin found, manner Homicide, noting "elements of positional and mechanical asphyxiation."
Family-retained pathologists (Drs. Baden and Wilson; law-firm email filed as a court exhibit): "traumatic/mechanical asphyxia." They did not testify at the Chauvin trial.

floyd-79.title: Detail
lines: Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), April 17, 2021, Brooklyn Center.

Quoted in H.Res. 331 (117th Cong.): "We're looking for a guilty verdict" and "Stay on the street, and we've got to get more active, we've got to get more confrontational, we've got to make sure they know we mean business."
Judge Cahill, April 19, 2021, on the record (as quoted in H.Res. 331 and the court video carried by CNN):
"I'll give you that Congresswoman Waters may have given you something on appeal that may result in this whole trial being overturned."
more: "I wish elected officials would stop talking about this case, especially in a manner that is disrespectful to the rule of law and to the judicial branch and our function … Their failure to do so I think is abhorrent."
"A congresswoman's opinion really doesn't matter a whole lot."
The mistrial motion was denied. H.Res. 331 (censure) was tabled 216–210 on April 20, 2021 (House roll call 122).
Chauvin's appellate brief raised the remarks. The COA affirmed without separately analyzing them.

President Biden, April 20, 2021 (Oval Office, official remarks): "I'm praying the verdict is the right verdict, which is—I think it's overwhelming, in my view. I wouldn't say that unless the jury was sequestered now and not hearing me say that." The jury had been fully sequestered for deliberations since April 19 under the court's order.
$27 million settlement, March 12, 2021: two seated jurors were excused and the venue/continuance requests renewed and denied (COA).
Venue and sequestration: see §§ 1.2 and 1.5.
